title: From Note G to WebAssembly
dek: Two centuries of turning text into running programs: the first interpreters and compilers, the theory of grammars and automata, optimisers, virtual machines and JITs, and the browser as a compilation target. Filter by chapter to follow one thread.

eras.title: Before compilers
eras.text: Programs are written as numbers, or wired by hand. Then they start living in memory, and the first interpreters appear.

eras.title: The first compilers
eras.text: Translating formulas into machine code automatically, and convincing programmers that the result can be fast.

eras.title: Theory meets practice
eras.text: Grammars, automata and types give compilers a mathematical foundation; Lex and Yacc make them easier to build.

eras.title: Optimising and portable
eras.text: Register allocation, SSA and free compilers; dynamic languages learn to compile themselves on the fly.

eras.title: Virtual machines and JITs
eras.text: Bytecode becomes mainstream with Java, and just-in-time compilers make dynamic languages fast.

eras.label: 2010 – today
eras.title: The browser as a target
eras.text: Compilers that compile themselves, languages that compile to JavaScript, and a portable bytecode for the web.

events.title: Note G
events.text: In her notes on Babbage's Analytical Engine, Lovelace writes out step by step how the machine would compute Bernoulli numbers, often called the first published program.

events.title: The stored-program computer
events.text: The First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC describes a machine whose program lives in memory alongside its data. Programs become data that other programs can write.

events.title: Short Code
events.text: Programmers write arithmetic expressions in a code that an interpreter carries out, at about fifty times the cost of machine code.

events.title: Regular events and finite automata
events.text: Studying nerve nets, Kleene shows that regular expressions describe exactly what finite automata recognise: the theory behind every lexer.

events.title: Autocode
events.text: For the Manchester Mark 1, often considered the first compiled programming language.

events.title: The A-0 system
events.text: Hopper's team at Remington Rand builds a system that assembles programs from a library of routines, and starts calling such tools “compilers”.

events.title: Three models for the description of language
events.text: Chomsky classifies grammars by their power. Context-free grammars, one level above regular ones, become the standard way of describing programming languages.

events.title: FORTRAN
events.who: John Backus and his team at IBM
events.text: The first FORTRAN compiler produces code nearly as fast as an expert's, and proves that high-level languages can be practical.

events.title: Lisp and the first eval
events.text: McCarthy defines Lisp through a function that evaluates Lisp; Russell implements it on the IBM 704, creating the first Lisp interpreter.

events.title: The ALGOL 60 report and BNF
events.who: John Backus, Peter Naur et al.
events.text: The syntax of a programming language is defined precisely, for the first time, with a grammar notation: Backus–Naur form.

events.title: A compiler that compiles itself
events.text: The Lisp 1.5 compiler is written in Lisp: the first self-hosting compiler.

events.title: LR parsing
events.text: Knuth defines the grammars that can be parsed bottom-up, deterministically, reading left to right: the LR(k) family.

events.title: From regular expressions to automata
events.text: Thompson's construction turns a regular expression into an automaton mechanically; it powers grep, editors and lexer generators.

events.title: Principal types
events.text: Every expression of combinatory logic has a most general type that can be computed: the seed of type inference.

events.title: Control flow analysis
events.text: Basic blocks and control-flow graphs: the framework every optimiser still uses. With John Cocke she publishes the catalogue of optimising transformations a year later.

events.title: C
events.text: A language close enough to the machine to write an operating system in. Unix is rewritten in C in 1973, and C becomes the portable assembler of the industry.

events.title: Top-down operator precedence
events.text: Binding powers instead of grammar levels: the expression-parsing method that Wahoo uses.

events.title: A unified approach to optimisation
events.text: Data-flow analyses become instances of one iterative framework over the control-flow graph.

events.title: Lex and Yacc
events.who: Mike Lesk, Eric Schmidt, Stephen Johnson
events.text: At Bell Labs, generators that write a lexer from regular expressions and an LALR parser from a grammar. Their descendants Flex and Bison are still used.

events.title: UCSD Pascal and p-code
events.text: Pascal compiled to bytecode for a virtual machine runs on many microcomputers: “write once, run anywhere” twenty years before Java.

events.title: A theory of type polymorphism
events.text: Algorithm W infers the most general types of a whole ML program without annotations. Haskell, OCaml and F# inherit it.

events.title: Register allocation by graph colouring
events.text: Values that are alive at the same time cannot share a register: allocating registers becomes colouring a graph.

events.title: Reflections on Trusting Trust
events.text: A compiler can hide a back door in every program it compiles, including itself, leaving no trace in any source code.

events.title: Dynamic translation of Smalltalk
events.text: Bytecode is translated to machine code when a method is first called, and cached: an ancestor of just-in-time compilation.

events.title: GCC 1.0
events.text: A free, retargetable optimising C compiler. It grows into the GNU Compiler Collection.

events.title: Static single assignment
events.who: Barry Rosen, Mark Wegman, Kenneth Zadeck
events.text: Every variable assigned exactly once: the intermediate form that nearly every optimising compiler uses today.

events.title: Polymorphic inline caches
events.who: Urs Hölzle, Craig Chambers, David Ungar
events.text: The Self project learns to optimise dynamic code from the types it actually sees: the techniques behind HotSpot and V8.

events.title: Python 0.9
events.text: A dynamic language compiled to bytecode for a virtual machine, which becomes one of the most used languages in the world.

events.title: Java and JavaScript
events.text: Java ships portable bytecode for the JVM; JavaScript, written in ten days, is interpreted inside Netscape Navigator.

events.title: HotSpot
events.who: Sun Microsystems (from the Self and Strongtalk team)
events.text: A JVM that interprets first and compiles only the hot methods, with optimisations based on what the program actually does.

events.title: LLVM 1.0
events.text: A reusable optimiser and back end around a well-defined SSA IR. Clang, Rust, Swift and Zig are built on it.

events.title: GCC drops its generated C++ parser
events.text: GCC 3.4 replaces its Bison grammar for C++ with a hand-written recursive-descent parser; the C front end follows in 2006.

events.title: V8
events.who: Lars Bak and the Chrome team
events.text: JavaScript compiled straight to machine code makes web applications fast enough to replace desktop software.

events.title: Rust compiles itself
events.who: Graydon Hoare and the Rust team
events.text: The Rust compiler, first written in OCaml, is rewritten in Rust and bootstraps itself. Rust 1.0 follows in 2015.

events.title: TypeScript
events.text: A typed language that compiles to JavaScript: the type checker catches errors, then the types are erased.

events.title: asm.js
events.who: Luke Wagner, Alon Zakai, David Herman (Mozilla)
events.text: A strict subset of JavaScript that engines can compile ahead of time shows that C and C++ can run in the browser at near-native speed.

events.title: Compiler errors for humans
events.text: Elm redesigns its error messages as plain explanations with suggestions; Rust and others follow, and Wahoo's messages copy the recipe.

events.title: Go compiles itself
events.text: Go 1.5 removes the last C from its compiler and runtime, translated to Go mostly by a program.

events.title: WebAssembly ships
events.text: A portable, validated bytecode, designed together by all four browser makers, runs in Firefox, Chrome, Edge and Safari.

events.title: Tree-sitter
events.text: An incremental parser generator that re-parses code as you type and gives editors accurate syntax trees.

events.title: WebAssembly becomes a W3C Recommendation
events.text: The fourth language of the web, after HTML, CSS and JavaScript.

events.title: A JIT for CPython
events.who: Brandt Bucher and the CPython team
events.text: Python 3.13 includes an experimental copy-and-patch JIT compiler, disabled by default: the reference Python starts compiling to machine code.

events.title: Wahoo
events.text: A compiler from the Mushroom Kingdom to WebAssembly, written in Rust, running in your browser. Try it in the playground.
